appraisal_events.evidence: «Rachel, quand je m'approchai d'elle, ne subit pas un moindre pouvoir de destruction... Ce n'était plus elle, je ne la reconnaissais que grâce à ses yeux... je ne distinguais plus que des protubérances, des taches, des fondrières.»
appraisal_events.explanation: Seen close up on the stage, Rachel is stripped of the beauty distance lent her and reduced, exactly like the painted flats beside her, to a disfigured surface; the narrator states this demolition in his own voice, without irony or reservation.

appraisal_events.evidence: «Ainsi il m'avait reconnu !» ; «cette fiction qu'il avait adoptée à ce moment-là, de ne pas me reconnaître, avait dû lui simplifier beaucoup les choses» ; «son corps avait été admirablement dressé par l'éducation à un certain nombre de dissimulations de bienséance et, comme un parfait comédien, il pouvait... jouer l'un après l'autre des rôles différents» ; «Saint-Loup s'imagina que sa maîtresse faisait attention à ce danseur... et sa figure se rembrunit.»
appraisal_events.explanation: Saint-Loup's apology retroactively converts his impersonal military salute into a deliberate social fiction, and the narrator's admiring vocabulary (admirablement dressé, parfait comédien) is turned into the instrument of exposure: what is praised is a caste-trained gift for cutting a friend without a flicker. The closing jealousy over the dancer extends the same movement, showing him governed by an illusion the narrator has just dismantled.

status_effects.explanation: Her local standing collapses: the prestige she held as a luminous stage figure is explicitly destroyed at close range and equated with cheap scenery.
He comes off worse because his warmth is revealed to be one role among several, interchangeable with a stranger's correctness that his training can produce instantly.
The passage ends with him darkening in jealousy over an imagined glance from Rachel toward the dancer, leaving him emotionally dependent on the very woman the narrator has just seen dissolve.

ambiguities: The stance toward Saint-Loup is layered: «admirablement dressé» and «parfait comédien» read on the surface as admiration for aristocratic self-command, and the restored fraternal bond («mon frère, il l'avait été, il l'était redevenu») partly rehabilitates him. The reading adopted here treats the praise as ironized exposure, since the whole analysis is triggered by the narrator's shock at having been cut in the street.

The narrator's own position is mildly positive (he is «heureux d'être là» and «charmé» by the Watteau-like dancer), but this aesthetic pleasure is not staged as a social or evaluative movement and is not recorded as an event.
